conceptual assets.information: The operation, target address, and write data of a debug-module access received over JTAG and issued through the DMI request interface; DMI reads and writes depend on it.
conceptual assets.rubric reason: The request is captured in the scan register, decoded into controller fields, and driven to the DMI request output, so modifying those elements can change the issued operation, address, or data (lines 196, 266-269, 283-285). The controller accepts a request only when it is not busy and the scanned operation is valid, so its gating can withhold a required DMI transfer (lines 264-271).
conceptual assets.attack: Alter the scanned command or the controller fields to redirect or corrupt a DMI access, or keep the controller busy so no request is issued.

conceptual assets.information: Data returned by the debug module for a DMI access and serialized to JTAG; debugger read operations depend on this information to report the accessed value.
conceptual assets.rubric reason: DMI response data is registered, placed into the DMI scan word, and shifted onto jtag_tdo_o, allowing the integration-level JTAG path to observe it (lines 274, 229, 189, 209). The response is stored and shifted through mutable scan and controller state, so corruption of those elements can change the returned value (lines 274, 189, 196, 209). Response capture and completion are gated by the busy and acknowledge handling, so those elements can withhold a required readback (lines 250, 273-276, 202-209).
conceptual assets.attack: Observe jtag_tdo_o to obtain returned debug data, corrupt the response or scan registers to produce a false value, or prevent capture and shifting so the readback is withheld.

conceptual assets.information: The internal busy state indicating that a DMI request has been issued and its response is pending; controller behavior depends on it to prevent overlapping transactions and capture completion. It has no entry or exit port because JTAG and response acknowledge values only decide this state rather than crossing into or out of it as data.
conceptual assets.rubric reason: The registered busy state controls request acceptance, response capture, and completion, so changing its set or clear behavior can cause overlapping or prematurely completed DMI transactions (lines 250, 264, 270, 276). A stuck or incorrectly cleared busy state can block new requests or prevent the pending response from being handled (lines 250, 264, 273-277).
conceptual assets.attack: Force the busy state high to stall all later accesses or clear it early to permit an overlapping request and corrupt transaction sequencing.

conceptual assets.information: The error indication generated when a DMI access is triggered while another access is busy and returned through the DTMCS or DMI scan data; debugger behavior depends on it to distinguish an invalid or failed protocol event.
conceptual assets.rubric reason: The error status is stored in dmi_ctrl.err, packed into the scan results, and returned through JTAG, so modifying it can make the debugger accept a failed access or report a false error (lines 241, 257-259, 224, 229, 188-189, 208-209).
conceptual assets.attack: Force the error state clear or set so software misclassifies a rejected DMI access as successful or treats a valid access as failed.

considered, not kept.reason: The dmireset and dmihardreset values only request or control reset behavior in the DMI controller, which the reset-path rule excludes as a conceptual asset (lines 247-252, 256).
The acknowledge field only completes and clears the in-progress transaction; it is handshake timing information rather than an independent asset (lines 275-277).
The TAP state register only orders scan steps and is sequencing state, which is explicitly excluded as information of its own (lines 119-142).
The trigger is a one-cycle timing pulse used to initiate a scan update and is pacing or sequencing information rather than an independent asset (lines 151-161).
The synchronizer stages and edge-detection signals only resample and pace the JTAG transfer, so synchronizer and pacing rules exclude them as separate information (lines 94-111).
The value is fixed from build-time generic constants and only identifies the implementation, with no demonstrated confidentiality, integrity, or availability objective (lines 21-23, 187, 207).
The bypass register only relays scan data from TDI to TDO and does not store, compute, or control a separately security-relevant value (lines 197, 210).
